excerpt: The injuries rear-end collisions cause most often, why symptoms can take days to appear, and what that delay does to a claim.
keyTakeaways: Rear-end collisions made up about 28.5% of police-reported U.S. crashes in 2023 (NHTSA) and commonly cause whiplash and other neck and back injuries, and sometimes concussions — symptoms that can take hours or days to appear. The rear driver is often found at fault because Georgia and South Carolina law both bar following too closely, but neither state presumes fault — it is decided on the facts. Victims can recover compensation for medical expenses, lost wages, pain and suffering, and more. Seeking immediate medical attention is essential for both your health and your injury claim.

faqs.question: What is the most common injury from a rear-end collision?
faqs.answer: Whiplash is the most common injury from a rear-end collision. It occurs when the head is violently thrown backward and then forward upon impact, stretching and tearing the muscles, tendons, and ligaments in the neck. About half of people with whiplash still report symptoms a year after the injury.

faqs.question: Can I still recover compensation if my injuries did not appear right away?
faqs.answer: Yes. Delayed symptoms are common after rear-end accidents: the stress response can blunt pain at first, and whiplash and concussion symptoms often take hours or a few days to appear. If you get medical care promptly and your records connect the injuries to the crash, you can pursue a claim for delayed-onset injuries within the filing deadline: 2 years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33), which runs from the crash date, not from when symptoms appear, and 3 years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530).

faqs.question: Who is at fault in a rear-end accident?
faqs.answer: The rear driver is usually found at fault, because Georgia and South Carolina law both require drivers to keep a reasonable and prudent following distance (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-49; S.C. Code § 56-5-1930). But neither state presumes fault from a rear-end impact: the rear driver may argue that the lead driver contributed to the crash through sudden unexpected braking, non-functioning brake lights, or reversing into the rear vehicle.

faqs.question: Can a low-speed rear-end collision cause serious injuries?
faqs.answer: Yes. Even lower-speed rear-end crashes can cause whiplash and other soft tissue injuries — neck sprains and strains are the most frequently reported injuries in U.S. auto insurance claims, according to IIHS. The severity depends on factors like vehicle size differences, headrest position, and whether the occupant was braced for impact. Never assume a low-speed collision is harmless.

faqs.question: What compensation can I recover after a rear-end accident?
faqs.answer: You may recover compensation for past and future medical expenses, lost wages and lost earning capacity, pain and suffering, emotional distress, loss of enjoyment of life, and property damage. In cases involving egregious conduct like drunk driving, punitive damages may also be available.

faqs.question: Should I see a doctor even if I feel fine after being rear-ended?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. Many rear-end collision injuries — including whiplash, concussions, and herniated discs — produce delayed symptoms that may not appear for hours or days. Seeking immediate medical evaluation protects your health and creates documented evidence linking the accident to your injuries, which is critical for any future injury claim.
